auto_merge.commit_message:
* `dict.popitem()`
* `dict.keys()`
* `dict.values()`
* `dict.items()`

Adds the "hidden" builtin types "dict_keys", "dict_values" and "dict_items" that live outside of the builtin scope.
auto_merge.commit_title: Improve return type inference of some builtin methods (GH-7888)

repo.description: The most widely used Python to C compiler
repo.name: cython

body:
This PR introduces return type inference of the following methods:
* [x]  `dict.popitem()`
* [x] `dict.keys()`
* [x] `dict.values()`
* [x] `dict.items()`
* [x] Avoid registering type to builtin scope
* [ ] Test the return type parsing in `TestBuiltin.TestBuiltinReturnTypes` and adapt the return type tests

> [!NOTE]
> based on #7887

comment_data.body: This defines the three types as user visible builtins. They should not be user visible because there is no such type in Python's type system. We can define them as types (internally), but we shouldn't register them in the builtins scope (or any scope at all, I guess).
We should do these replacements later, after splitting the string below, when mapping type names to types. String replacements seem inherently unsafe here.

+            if return_type_name == 'K' and container_type.is_pyanydict_type:
+                return builtin_type.infer_iterator_type() or PyrexTypes.py_object_type
             if 'T' in subscripted_type_names:
                 subscripted_type_names = subscripted_type_names.replace('T', builtin_type.name)
+            if 'I' in subscripted_type_names:

+def _parse_atomic_signature(builtin_type, sig: str) -> PyrexTypes.PyrexType:

+    if sig == 'I':

comment_data.body:
> This defines the three types as user visible builtins

What does it exactly mean "visible"? The user see it:

```python
d = {"a": 1}
k = d.keys()

type(k)
# <class 'dict_keys'>
```

And can be used in `isinstance()`:
```python
isinstance(k, type(d.keys()))  # True
```

but **cannot be created manually** only via `keys()` (and friends).

Not sure if it counts as "part of Python's type system or not". This type is kind of mentioned also in [python docs](https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com#dictionary-view-objects).

In any case, current code needs to search the type in builtin scope (at least this PR)- e.g.: here:

https://github.com/cython/cython/pull/7888/files#r3740733070

Hence we have two possibilities:
* keep new `dict_*` types in `builtin_scope` and the rest of code can search the type dynamically from it`
* create the types manually in `PyrexTypes` and hard code them across code base (at least in https://github.com/cython/cython/pull/7888/files#r3740733070)

Not sure what is better approach. I don't know what are all implications of having the type in builtin scope so I cannot tell what is better... :-(

The way you declared them, users can write `k = dict_keys()` and `isinstance(k, dict_keys)` etc. That's probably not intended and definitely not good. The type names should not be user visible.

I think we need to construct the types manually like the other (C-) types in `PyrexTypes.py`, and not add them to a scope at all. At least, that's what I'd try.

I wrongly wrote "no such type in Python's type system" above, but what I actually meant was "not in Python's builtins". I'm only referring to the names of the types, not the types themselves. We clearly need the types for the return type declarations, so they need to exist, but they should not be part of the builtin scope (or any other scope) and it should not be possible for _users_ to use them as types. It should not be possible to look them up by name. I hope it's clearer now.

```suggestion
# 'I' - type of index type:
#     - value type from subscript - e.g. for list[int], I is `int`
#     - for mappings this is the second subscripted type - e.g. for dict[int, str], I is `str`
# 'K' - key type of dictionary - e.g. for dict[int, str], K is `int`
```

@@ -496,7 +502,12 @@ def _generate_divmod_function(scope, argument_types):
 # When updating this mapping, also update "unsafe_compile_time_methods" below
 # if methods are added that are not safe to evaluate at compile time.
 # 'T' - type identical to type in dictionary key
-# 'I' - type from subscript - e.g. for list[int], I is `int`
+# 'I' - type of index type:
+#     - for no-dict it is type from subscript - e.g. for list[int], I is `int`
+#     - for dict it is second subscripted type - e.g. for dict[int, str],
+#       I is `str`
+# 'K' - key value type of dictionary - second subscripted type
+#     - e.g. for dict[int, str], v is `str`
